title: CT head — bone window
region: Skull vault, skull base and paranasal sinuses
sideNote: Conventional axial display: the patient's right is on the viewer's left. No side marker is burned into the image, and the source PACS annotation carrying patient identifiers has been cropped away entirely.
markers: Axial · patient right on viewer left
provenance: Reconstructed from a screen recording of a PACS session. 827 frames collapsed to 55 distinct images, deduplicated across the reader's two scroll passes to 33 unique levels, ordered by spectral seriation of the slice-similarity graph with 2-opt and or-opt refinement, then cropped to the image itself. Every burned-in patient identifier — name, date of birth, accession number, institution — lies outside the crop, verified by counting coloured pixels in the published slices: zero.

levels.label: Sella, sphenoid sinus and petrous apex
Internal acoustic meatus and skull base foramina
Foramen magnum, nasal cavity and C1

structures.name: Frontal sinus
structures.recognition: Air-filled cavity in the frontal bone above the orbits, often asymmetrical with a bony septum off the midline. It is the most superior of the paranasal sinuses and is absent in small children.

structures.name: Ethmoid air cells
structures.recognition: A honeycomb of small air cells between the orbits, bounded laterally by the paper-thin lamina papyracea. Divided into anterior, middle and posterior groups.

structures.name: Sphenoid sinus
structures.recognition: Single large midline air space in the body of the sphenoid, directly below the sella turcica and in front of the clivus. It is the surgical route to the pituitary.

structures.name: Maxillary sinus
structures.recognition: The largest paranasal sinus, a pyramid in the maxilla lateral to the nasal cavity. Its ostium sits high on the medial wall, which is why it drains poorly when the patient is upright.

structures.name: Mastoid air cells
structures.recognition: Lucent honeycomb in the mastoid process behind the external auditory canal, continuous with the middle ear through the aditus and antrum — which is why otitis media spreads here.

structures.name: Petrous temporal bone
structures.recognition: The dense wedge of bone pointing anteromedially towards the sella, separating middle from posterior cranial fossa and containing the inner ear.

structures.name: Internal acoustic meatus
structures.recognition: A short horizontal canal running laterally from the posterior surface of the petrous bone into it, carrying the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves. Look for a paired, symmetrical tube pointing at the internal ear.

structures.name: Carotid canal
structures.recognition: Round lucency in the petrous bone anteromedial to the middle ear, turning from vertical to horizontal as it carries the internal carotid artery towards the cavernous sinus.

structures.name: Jugular foramen
structures.recognition: Larger, more posterior and usually right-dominant opening behind the carotid canal, transmitting the internal jugular vein with cranial nerves IX, X and XI.

structures.name: Foramen ovale
structures.recognition: Oval lucency in the greater wing of the sphenoid carrying the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Foramen spinosum sits just posterolateral to it and is smaller and rounder.

structures.name: Foramen spinosum
structures.recognition: Small round hole posterolateral to foramen ovale, transmitting the middle meningeal artery — the vessel torn in an extradural haematoma.

structures.name: Foramen magnum
structures.recognition: The largest opening in the skull base, bounded by the occipital bone, transmitting the medulla, vertebral arteries and the spinal roots of the accessory nerve.

structures.name: Sella turcica
structures.recognition: The saddle-shaped hollow on the upper surface of the sphenoid body holding the pituitary, with the anterior and posterior clinoid processes at its corners and the sphenoid sinus directly beneath.

structures.name: Clivus
structures.recognition: The sloping bony ramp behind the sphenoid sinus formed by the fused basisphenoid and basiocciput, running down to the foramen magnum with the brainstem lying against it.

structures.name: Crista galli
structures.recognition: Midline bony ridge of the ethmoid projecting up into the anterior cranial fossa, the anchor for the falx cerebri, with the cribriform plate on either side of it.

structures.name: Nasal septum
structures.recognition: Midline partition of the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid above and the vomer below, with the septal cartilage anteriorly. Deviation is extremely common and usually of no consequence.

structures.name: External acoustic meatus
structures.recognition: Air-filled canal running laterally to the skin surface, in line with the middle ear. Distinguish it from the internal acoustic meatus, which points medially into the petrous bone.

structures.name: Coronal suture
structures.recognition: Runs transversely between frontal and parietal bones. On axial slices it appears as a symmetrical pair of oblique lucencies in the anterior vault, sloping backwards as you move down the stack.

structures.name: Lambdoid suture
structures.recognition: Between the parietal bones and the occipital bone posteriorly, forming an inverted V. More serrated than the coronal suture and often contains wormian bones.

structures.name: Sagittal suture
structures.recognition: Strictly midline between the two parietal bones, seen only on the highest slices. Do not confuse it with a fracture: a suture is serrated, symmetrical and has sclerotic margins.

structures.name: Squamosal suture
structures.recognition: Arches over the squamous temporal bone where it overlaps the parietal, a shallow bevelled joint on the lateral vault rather than a serrated one.

structures.name: Orbit
structures.recognition: Bony pyramid with its apex at the optic canal. The medial wall is the paper-thin lamina papyracea against the ethmoid, the floor is the roof of the maxillary sinus — the two walls that blow out.

structures.name: Calvarium
structures.recognition: Inner and outer tables of dense cortical bone with the diploic space of marrow between them. Losing the distinction between the three layers is what makes a lytic lesion visible.
